title: Get started
description: Requirements, installation, and the first steps for a Troolio host.
text:
Get started 
 Troolio 10.0.8 is a .NET 10 framework for event-sourced actors on Microsoft Orleans 10. This path gets you from a package reference to a small actor, then points to the host and provider decisions that make a real application work. On this page Before you begin Install the foundation Follow the first application path What the package does and what the host does Run a complete sample 
 Before you begin 
 
 Install the .NET 10 SDK. Use a .NET 10 runtime for the host. 
 Keep Microsoft Orleans packages on the 10.x line across the application. 
 Review and accept the license included in each Troolio package. 
 Decide whether this is a local learning host or a serving application. In-memory storage is useful for local examples and loses data on process exit. 
 
 Install the foundation 
 Create a project, then add the framework and Orleans build tooling. The exact version avoids mixing the five-package cohort with older builds. 
 dotnet new classlib -n MyApp -f net10.0
cd MyApp
dotnet add package Troolio.Core --version 10.0.8
dotnet add package Microsoft.Orleans.Sdk --version 10.0.0
 
 Add a provider only when the host needs it: 
 dotnet add package Troolio.SqlServer --version 10.0.8
# or
dotnet add package Troolio.KurrentDB --version 10.0.8
 
 Use the  package guide  for the roles and dependencies of all five packages. A SQL Server or KurrentDB reference does not install a production schema or select a serving route. 
 Follow the first application path 
 
 See how Troolio works , then  model a command  and  build your first actor  with a command, an event, an event handler, and a query. The guide shows the 10.0.8 actor API. 
 Configure a host  with actor assembly registration, a store, a serializer, and Orleans services. 
 Read  actors and commands  and  events and state  before choosing a persistence provider. 
 For an explicitly selected atomic path, review  the selected command route  and  atomic commit  together. The route needs compatible store capabilities, authority, projection handoffs, and recovery. 
 Plan for  security and retention  and  deployment  before serving real callers. 
 
 What the package does and what the host does 
 Troolio supplies actor and event contracts, command dispatch, storage abstractions, and opt-in provider surfaces. The application host authenticates callers, authorizes the current command and target, configures credentials, selects a route, operates projection and recovery workers, and sets evidence and idempotency retention windows. Installing a package by itself activates none of those decisions. 
 Run a complete sample 
 Start with  Calculator , continue with the  ToDo API , then explore  Shopping List . The examples use public packages and include host setup, source code and storage boundaries.  Packages  describes the framework and optional extension version lines.

title: How Troolio works
description: A visual tour of commands, events, state, projections, and routes.
text:
How Troolio works 
 Troolio helps you represent a business action as a  command , record its outcome as an  event , and answer questions from state rebuilt from those events. It runs on Microsoft Orleans actors. You can start with one actor and add projections or provider adapters as your application grows. On this page One actor, four ideas What readers and outside systems see Choose a command path Where to go next Continue into an application 
 One actor, four ideas 
 
 A  command  asks an actor to do something, such as  Increment . 
 A  handler  checks the request and decides what happened. 
 An  event  records that fact, such as  Incremented . The event stream is the write history. 
 A  query  reads current state. On activation, the actor can rebuild that state by replaying its events. 
 
 
 In the  first actor , these two methods make the relationship concrete: 
 public IEnumerable<Event> Handle(Increment command) =>
    [new Incremented(command.Headers)];

public void On(Incremented _) => count++;
 
 The first method decides an event; the second applies it to state. Keep  On  free of network or provider calls so replay is safe. 
 What readers and outside systems see 
 A projection consumes committed events to build a read model. It can lag behind the command result. An external action, such as a reminder or notification, needs a durable effect intent and a provider that deduplicates retries. 
 
 Projections  and  external effects  explain the two paths. 
 Choose a command path 
 For a first app, learn the ordinary actor path and configure a suitable store. For an operation whose participants, projection handoffs, and completion evidence must commit together, explicitly select the  atomic command route . That route requires a compatible store, current route authority, and recovery plan; a package reference does not activate it. 
 Where to go next 
 
 Model a command and rule  with an accepted and rejected outcome. 
 Build the first actor , then  configure the host . 
 Explore  events and state ,  stores , and  read models . 
 For advanced routes, follow  atomic commit ,  route authority , and  recovery . 
 
 Continue into an application 
 Follow the  workshop workflow  to connect two actors, orchestration, a SQL projection, and an authorized reader. Learn  message metadata  to understand correlation, causation, user, device, message, and transaction IDs.

title: Client calls and routing
description: Send actor messages and configure a cluster client.
text:
Client calls and routing 
 ITroolioClient  is the application-facing client contract for addressing actors and fetching read models.  Tell<TActor>  sends a typed actor message to an actor ID.  Ask<TActor,TResult>  sends a typed message and awaits a result.  Get<TReadModel>  resolves a read model by ID. The interface does not authenticate or authorize a business command for you; enforce those rules before calling it. On this page Register the client Delivery semantics Example: Tell an actor and read a view 
 Register the client 
 TroolioClientExtensions.AddTroolioClient  registers a singleton client using the application name and actor assemblies. The current implementation reads  appsettings.json , optional environment-specific JSON files, and environment variables. With  <appName>:Clustering:Storage  set to  Local , it uses demo clustering. Otherwise it configures an Azure Storage gateway from  <appName>:Clustering:ConnectionString . Review that choice for the deployment and keep its credential out of source control. 
 The client constructor starts Orleans hosted services and connects to the cluster. Treat client creation as an application startup step, account for connection failures, and verify shutdown behavior in your host.  IActorSystemExtensions.ActorOf<TActor>(id)  and  Worker<TActor>()  offer typed actor references inside code that already has an actor system. 
 Delivery semantics 
 A successful  Tell  indicates that the client call completed, not that a selected atomic transaction and every downstream projection completed. For commands requiring an authoritative outcome, use a response or operation receipt and the appropriate  selected route . Queries can observe a current actor state while  read models  lag behind the event commit. 
 Example: Tell an actor and read a view 
 The client addresses a typed actor by ID. A read model query uses its own ID and may observe a later projection state. 
 public static Task Send(ITroolioClient client, Metadata headers) =>
    client.Tell<ICounterActor>("42", new Increment(headers));
 
 public static async Task<int> ReadProjection(ITroolioClient client) =>
    (await client.Get<CounterReadModel>("d1cb4bc0-114d-4a8c-9a5e-f460784d7340")).Count;

title: Actors and commands
description: Actor roles, typed commands, queries, and dispatch.
text:
Actors and commands 
 Troolio uses Microsoft Orleans actors as the command boundary. An actor interface extends  IActor ; a concrete actor handles typed messages and keeps the current state derived from its event history.  CqrsActor ,  EventSourcedActor ,  StatefulActor ,  ProjectionActor , and  OrchestrationActor  serve different roles rather than interchangeable base classes. On this page Command path Actor roles Ordinary and selected command paths Design checks Example: Send a typed command Choosing a real application boundary 
 Command path 
 A  Command<TActor>  addresses a specific actor contract. A handler named  Handle  returns zero or more domain events. The actor dispatches those events to  On  handlers to update its in-memory state. Queries use  Query<TActor,TResult>  and a typed handler to read that current state.  The first actor guide  has a compiled example. 
 InternalCommand<TActor>  is used for framework and orchestration work inside the actor system. A serving host still has to decide which external commands it permits, authenticate the caller, and authorize the target. Message  Metadata  carries correlation and identity fields; it is trace context, not proof of current authorization. 
 Actor roles 
 
 
 
 Role 
 Typical responsibility 
 
 
 
 
 Event sourced actor 
 Replays a stream, handles commands, emits events, and answers queries. 
 
 
 Stateful actor 
 Maintains state from subscribed events for internal orchestration. 
 
 
 Projection actor 
 Consumes events to update a read model outside the command transaction. 
 
 
 Orchestration actor 
 Reacts to events and may issue internal commands. 
 
 
 Dispatch actor 
 Provides typed message dispatch without selecting a persistence policy. 
 
 
 
 Ordinary and selected command paths 
 The ordinary actor path appends to its configured store and dispatches events according to host configuration. A separately selected atomic path plans a closed participant set and requires a capable transaction store, route authority, and completion receipt. Do not infer selected-route guarantees from an ordinary  Command  call. Read  selected command route  before using it. 
 Design checks 
 
 Keep command handlers focused on deciding events. Historical event replay must be free of external side effects. 
 Treat an empty event result as a meaningful no-change outcome only when the selected route's completion store supports it. 
 Use stable actor IDs and version expectations. A store rejects stale expected versions rather than silently overwriting history. 
 
 Example: Send a typed command 
 Using the counter actor from the  first actor guide , a client addresses one actor ID and sends its command. The host still authorizes the caller and target. 
 public static Task Send(ITroolioClient client, Metadata headers) =>
    client.Tell<ICounterActor>("42", new Increment(headers));
 
 Choosing a real application boundary 
 Use  actor boundaries and identity  to place invariants and stable keys, then follow  CQRS in practice  to choose between actor queries and semantic SQL views.

title: Events and state
description: Event history, state replay, and lifecycle.
text:
Events, state, and snapshots 
 An event records an accepted domain fact. The event stream is the actor's write history; its current in-memory state is rebuilt by applying that history. A read model is another view over relevant facts, optimized for the reader that uses it. On this page Keep event application pure Message and source identity Typed state and creation Snapshots Evolve history deliberately 
 In the workshop example,  RegistrationRequested  records the workshop, attendee, and display name.  RegistrationCancelled  records the cancelled result. Applying those events produces the current registration state. 
 Keep event application pure 
 [GenerateSerializer]
public record RegistrationState(Guid RegistrationId, Guid WorkshopId,
    Guid AttendeeId, string DisplayName, string Status) : IActorState
{
    public static RegistrationState Empty => new(Guid.Empty, Guid.Empty,
        Guid.Empty, "", "absent");

    public RegistrationState Apply(RegistrationRequested e) =>
        new(e.RegistrationId, e.WorkshopId, e.AttendeeId, e.DisplayName, "requested");

    public RegistrationState Apply(RegistrationCancelled e) =>
        new(e.RegistrationId, e.WorkshopId, e.AttendeeId, e.DisplayName, "cancelled");
}
 
 These methods return a new state record. They do not send commands, query SQL, or call a provider. The actor can apply historical events during activation and recover the same state without repeating outside work. 
 The command handler has another job: validate intent against current state and decide events. The projection and orchestration listeners handle their configured event delivery separately.  Replay and live events  shows that separation visually. 
 Message and source identity 
 Event  carries  Metadata , including correlation, causation, user, device, message, and transaction IDs. Those fields explain attribution and relationships. They do not alone establish current authorization or projection deduplication. 
 EventEnvelope<T>  adds a source locator: 
 
 
 
 Field 
 Meaning 
 
 
 
 
 Id 
 The source actor's key. It is not a per-event UUID. 
 
 
 Stream 
 The source stream name. 
 
 
 Version 
 The source position under the producer/provider's version contract. 
 
 
 Event 
 The typed domain event and its metadata. 
 
 
 
 A listener can combine stream and version with its consumer identity to recognize a delivered source. Filtered events and framework records can affect which version values a particular consumer sees, so do not assume every observed number is consecutive. 
 For the full explanation of the six header fields and current dispatch behavior, read  message metadata  and  correlation and causation . 
 Typed state and creation 
 EventSourcedActor<TState>  and  StatefulActor<TState>  provide typed state shapes.  CreatableActor  adds an explicit creation lifecycle for actors that use a create command. An actor reference can exist before the corresponding domain entity exists; define what each command does in that state. 
 Use stable actor IDs and reject conflicting reuse. A cancellation or retirement may also need durable lifecycle evidence so delayed work cannot recreate the entity accidentally.  Actor boundaries  and  idempotency  explore those choices. 
 Snapshots 
 Snapshots can reduce replay work for a compatible actor/store path. They must remain tied to committed event history and the state schema. They are not a replacement for event history or a signal that all external projections are current. Authority-sensitive source-observation paths can bypass legacy snapshots. 
 The generic event-sourced actor reads its configured snapshot policy; a serving host must still choose appropriate retention, serializer compatibility, and recovery behavior. A snapshot should not contain prospective uncommitted state or become an independent source of business authority. 
 Evolve history deliberately 
 Changing a C# record does not rewrite stored events. Keep historical event types and payloads readable, version the persisted format where needed, and replay representative histories before introducing new writers. 
 Records provide useful value semantics, but mutable nested lists or arrays can still change after construction. Use immutable collections or defensively copy retained payloads, particularly before asynchronous persistence. 
 Continue with  stores and serialization ,  read-model design , and the  workshop walkthrough .

title: Stores and serialization
description: Persistence contracts and event formats.
text:
Stores and serialization 
 IStore  is the base event-stream contract. It appends a collection of events at an expected stream version and reads all, a range, the last event, or one event. A store implementation determines durability, concurrency behavior, and its deployment requirements. On this page Store choices Serializer options Operational contract Example: Append and serialize events 
 Store choices 
 
 
 
 Store 
 Intended use 
 
 
 
 
 InMemoryStore 
 Local examples and tests; state disappears with the process. 
 
 
 FileSystemStore 
 Local filesystem experiments; review filesystem semantics before relying on it. 
 
 
 Troolio.SqlServer 
 SQL Server adapters with explicit schema, transaction, and recovery setup. 
 
 
 Troolio.KurrentDB 
 KurrentDB append and named-stream integration with separate route and recovery contracts. 
 
 
 
 The two bundled Core stores do not grant the selected atomic transaction capability. That route requires  IAtomicEventTransactionStore  and, when fenced,  IRouteFencedAtomicEventTransactionStore  with the required capability flags.  Atomic commit  explains the full contract. 
 Serializer options 
 Core includes  JsonEventSerializer ,  MessagePackEventSerializer , and  MessagePackLz4EventSerializer  behind  IEventSerializer . Choose one deliberately, test round trips of your domain event types, and retain backward readers for any stored format you have already written. Changing serializers without migration can make historical replay fail. 
 Orleans serialization attributes on message records serve actor transport. They do not by themselves define the bytes your chosen event store writes. The store's serializer and the application event schema must agree. 
 Operational contract 
 The store must enforce expected versions and return an append count consistent with what it committed. For the selected route, the store must atomically commit participant events, required projection handoffs, ancillary writes, and completion evidence. A  IStore  implementation alone does not promise that stronger property. 
 Example: Append and serialize events 
 The application supplies a store and serializer. Use the stream’s actual current version;  0  below is only appropriate for a new stream. 
 public static byte[] SerializeEvent(
    Troolio.Core.Serialization.IEventSerializer serializer, Metadata headers) =>
    serializer.Serialize(new Incremented(headers));
 
 public static async Task<ulong> Append(IStore store, Metadata headers) =>
    await store.Append("CounterActor-42", 0,
        new IEvent[] { new Incremented(headers) });

title: Streams and subscriptions
description: Event streams, subscriptions, and queues.
text:
Streams and subscriptions 
 Troolio uses Orleans streams and broadcast channels to move event envelopes toward projection and orchestration consumers. Subscription attributes connect a consumer to events from an actor type or name; they are routing declarations, not a durable completion receipt. On this page Projection subscriptions Orchestration subscriptions When atomic closure is required Host responsibilities Example: Subscribe a projection 
 Projection subscriptions 
 ProjectionStreamSubscriptionAttribute  matches a projection stream namespace derived from an actor type or actor name. Projection actors resume stream subscriptions and process  IEventEnvelope  messages. The source actor's append can complete before the read model reflects that event; design callers for eventual consistency. 
 Orchestration subscriptions 
 OrchestrationStreamSubscriptionAttribute  serves orchestration listeners. An orchestration handler may issue internal commands that produce more events. A broadcast publish alone does not prove that every expected handler has finished, that nested work is registered, or that an event-only transaction is closed. 
 When atomic closure is required 
 Selected event-only routes require a reviewed subscriber manifest and a durable closure protocol. The manifest must account for the deployed binding inventory and handler effect classification. Completion receipts are recorded only after expected handlers and child work finish. Read  orchestration  and  selected command route  before using those surfaces. 
 Host responsibilities 
 Configure stream providers and subscription lifecycle in the host. Monitor consumer lag and recover pending durable handoffs. Keep a stable deployment/binding version during a selected route, and reject drift before commit. Do not use stream delivery as a substitute for store transaction guarantees. 
 Example: Subscribe a projection 
 This projection subscribes to streams produced by  CounterActor . The application writer must apply the event version idempotently and handle retries. 
 public interface ICounterProjectionWriter
{
    Task ApplyAsync(string actorId, ulong version);
}

[ProjectionStreamSubscription(typeof(CounterActor))]
public sealed class CounterProjection(ICounterProjectionWriter writer) : ProjectionActor
{
    public Task On(EventEnvelope<Incremented> envelope) =>
        writer.ApplyAsync(envelope.Id, envelope.Version);
}

title: Reliable jobs
description: Queue-backed jobs and reminder boundaries.
text:
Background jobs and queueing 
 Core includes a  BatchJobActor  and message queue abstractions for queued actor commands. Treat this as a separate background path from the selected atomic command transaction and external effect intent protocol. On this page Queue contract Retry boundaries Example: Add a queued item 
 Queue contract 
 IMessageQueueProvider  supplies a client for a named queue.  BatchJobActor  places a batch job on that queue, uses a timer and reminder to wake processing, and tracks dequeue attempts against the job's retry limit. The configured queue provider determines persistence, visibility, and failure behavior. 
 InMemoryMessageQueueProvider  is process-local and is appropriate for tests or local evaluation. It does not give a durable, multi-silo queue. A serving deployment must choose a provider with the retention and retry semantics it needs and prove the worker lifecycle under process loss. 
 Retry boundaries 
 A retry can repeat a command or provider call after an uncertain outcome. Use stable operation IDs and the selected route's exact completion evidence for business commands. For external effects, the provider must enforce durable idempotency and return terminal receipts for known outcomes. Queue attempt count alone is not an exactly-once guarantee. 
 Use  BatchJobActor  only after reviewing its queue provider and error handling for your deployment. 
 Example: Add a queued item 
 A queue provider supplies a named typed client. The example only shows enqueueing; production durability and worker behavior come from the configured provider. 
 public static async Task Enqueue(IMessageQueueProvider queues) =>
    await queues.GetClient<string>("notifications").Add("hello", TimeSpan.FromDays(1));

title: Message metadata
description: Understand every Metadata field, identity lifetime, and the current dispatch behavior.
text:
Message metadata 
 A message carries two kinds of information: the domain payload says what the application is doing, and its  Metadata  says how that work is related to a caller and other messages. For example,  RequestRegistration  contains a workshop ID and display name. Its headers carry the user, device, and identifiers used to follow the request. On this page The six fields Construct headers at the boundary What ordinary Troolio dispatch does User, owner, and recipient are different roles Transaction context and later jobs 
 The distinction matters when a request crosses actors or runs again after a failure. A registration ID is a business identity. A correlation ID groups related work. A message ID identifies a message in that work. They answer different questions and should be stored and logged separately. 
 The six fields 
 
 
 
 Field 
 Question it answers 
 Typical lifetime 
 
 
 
 
 CorrelationId 
 Which user interaction or workflow does this belong to? 
 Shared by related work in one chosen correlation scope. 
 
 
 MessageId 
 Which message or runtime dispatch is this? 
 Distinguishes messages within a correlation. 
 
 
 CausationId 
 Which message directly caused this message? 
 Parent link; normally absent at a root boundary. 
 
 
 UserId 
 Which user is attributed to this action? 
 Preserved as attribution when appropriate; verified at ingress. 
 
 
 DeviceId 
 Which client device/session context originated the action? 
 Shared across requests from that verified device context. 
 
 
 TransactionId 
 Which Troolio transaction context does this dispatch participate in? 
 Set by the command protocol; not chosen freely by a browser. 
 
 
 
 All six are  Guid  values;  CausationId  and  TransactionId  are nullable. The three-argument  Metadata  constructor creates a message ID for you. It does not prove that a user, device, or correlation scope is valid. 
 Construct headers at the boundary 
 The application authenticates the request and obtains the current user and device from its trusted session. It then constructs headers for a command. Keep the same correlation ID across the related work you want to investigate together. 
 public static Metadata AtIngress(Guid correlationId, Guid userId, Guid deviceId) =>
    new(correlationId, userId, deviceId);
 
 A client-supplied correlation ID can be useful for support, but validate its shape and decide whether to accept it or allocate a server value. An arbitrary client payload must not choose the effective  UserId  simply by setting a header. Likewise, possession of someone else's  DeviceId  is not a credential. 
 The workshop sample sends those headers with a typed command to the registration actor: 
 public static Task RequestAsync(ITroolioClient client, Guid registrationId, Guid workshopId,
    string displayName, Guid authenticatedUserId, Guid verifiedDeviceId, Guid correlationId)
{
    Metadata headers = MessageContext.AtIngress(correlationId, authenticatedUserId, verifiedDeviceId);
    return client.Tell<IRegistrationActor>(registrationId.ToString("D"),
        new RequestRegistration(headers, registrationId, workshopId, displayName));
}
 
 Use the registration ID as the actor key and business retry identity. It remains meaningful even if diagnostic message IDs change along the dispatch path. 
 What ordinary Troolio dispatch does 
 In the ordinary 10.0.8 command path, Troolio establishes a transaction ID and replaces the incoming command's message ID for runtime handling. When it prepares events, it creates event message IDs and sets their causation to the handled command's ID. An ordinary  InternalCommand  receives its own runtime message ID and takes causation from the message ID carried in its incoming headers. 
 That is why an orchestration listener forwards the triggering event's headers to an internal command. Let the command protocol establish the next step. The selected atomic path uses its verified operation identity and contextual rules; follow  the selected route  when using that path. 
 Trace-enabled projection and orchestration processing may also derive delivery headers. Therefore a subscriber should use the provider's source identity, such as stream and version, for durable deduplication. A diagnostic message ID is not a universal projection receipt key. 
 User, owner, and recipient are different roles 
 Imagine an administrator cancels a registration for an attendee. The acting user is the administrator; the registration's owner and confirmation recipient may be the attendee. Store those domain roles explicitly. Replacing  UserId  with the recipient destroys useful attribution and can obscure who authorized the operation. 
 Background work also needs an explicit policy. Retaining an initiating user's ID explains attribution, while current authorization still has to be checked before accessing data or changing state. A system actor is not automatically privileged because a header contains  Guid.Empty . 
 Transaction context and later jobs 
 An external command should enter with no caller-invented transaction ID. Internal work can carry the active context through orchestration. A scheduled job that runs much later starts a new transaction scope when it issues its own external command; it should not keep a completed transaction alive through old headers. 
 public static Metadata Scheduled(Metadata trigger, Guid currentUserId) =>
    new(Guid.NewGuid(), currentUserId, Guid.Empty)
    {
        CausationId = trigger.MessageId,
        TransactionId = null
    };
 
 This is an application policy for a later job, including a new correlation scope and a causal link to its trigger. Recheck the relevant authority when the job runs. Use a durable job or operation ID for retries. 
 Continue with  correlation and causation ,  actor identity , and  observability . The  workshop sample  defines the application helpers shown here.

title: Correlation and causation
description: Follow a branching workflow and distinguish diagnostics from durable retry identity.
text:
Correlation and causation 
 Correlation groups a story. Causation connects its individual steps. If a customer requests a workshop registration, that one interaction can cause a roster change, a read-model update, and a confirmation. They can share a correlation ID while each message has its own identity and immediate parent. On this page Walk through the chain Branching is normal Define where a story ends Retries need their own identity rules Correlation versus distributed traces 
 Without correlation, the same action looks like unrelated log entries. Without causation, a search finds related entries but cannot tell which message triggered which follow-up. 
 
 Walk through the chain 
 Consider this simplified runtime sequence. The letters represent IDs, not domain values. 
 
 
 
 Step 
 Message ID 
 Causation ID 
 Correlation ID 
 
 
 
 
 Runtime handles  RequestRegistration 
 A 
 Root context 
 R 
 
 
 Actor produces  RegistrationRequested 
 B 
 A 
 R 
 
 
 Roster actor handles  AddAttendee 
 C 
 B 
 R 
 
 
 Roster actor produces  AttendeeAdded 
 D 
 C 
 R 
 
 
 Application creates confirmation work 
 E 
 Its triggering message 
 R 
 
 
 
 The ordinary actor pipeline assigns command and event IDs as described in  message metadata . This table illustrates those semantic roles; delivery tracing can add further processing steps. Log both correlation and causation so a delayed or repeated message can be understood in context. 
 Branching is normal 
 One event can have several consumers. A projection updates a registration card while an orchestration changes another actor. Those branches have a shared ancestor. Causation refers to the immediate parent, so copying a correlation ID into  CausationId  loses the structure of the workflow. 
 For an application-owned message outside the actor dispatch protocol, a helper can make a child context explicitly: 
 public static Metadata Child(Metadata parent) => parent with
{
    MessageId = Guid.NewGuid(),
    CausationId = parent.MessageId
};
 
 The helper preserves correlation, user, device, and transaction context, creates the child message ID, and records the parent's ID. For an ordinary Troolio internal command, forward the triggering event's headers instead; the framework establishes the child command context during dispatch. Do not apply both conventions without understanding that extra processing hop. 
 Define where a story ends 
 A correlation scope is an application decision. A button click and its immediate outcomes make a useful scope. A recurring reminder tomorrow can start another scope and retain a causal reference to the scheduled trigger. A long-running business workflow may keep a separate workflow ID across many such interactions. 
 Avoid grouping every action by the same user under one permanent correlation ID. Support queries become noisy, and unrelated user actions look causally related. Conversely, allocating a fresh correlation ID at every actor hop makes one interaction difficult to follow. 
 Retries need their own identity rules 
 Suppose a client times out after the event commit. Sending a new request with a new correlation ID does not establish whether it should append again. Reusing the old correlation ID does not make it idempotent either. The decision belongs to the command's business identity and, for a selected route, its verified operation identity and exact request/batch evidence. 
 A registration actor can recognize a retry of the same registration details. A projection can recognize the same source stream/version. An effect provider can recognize a stable idempotency key. These mechanisms preserve correctness even when logs contain several attempts or tracing derives new processing message IDs. 
 Correlation versus distributed traces 
 CorrelationId  is a Troolio/application GUID. A W3C trace contains a trace ID and span IDs managed by the tracing system. They can be linked through tags and log scopes, but setting a correlation ID does not start an  Activity , propagate  traceparent , or create a tracing exporter. 
 Keep both when they serve different audiences: the application correlation ID connects the business interaction, while spans show execution timing and service calls. Use  observability  for the C# instrumentation pattern. 
 Continue with  orchestration workflows ,  idempotency and ordering , and  notifications .

title: CQRS in practice
description: Separate business decisions from query-shaped views and explain consistency to callers.
text:
CQRS in practice 
 CQRS gives commands and queries different jobs. A command asks the write side to decide a change. A query asks for information in a shape that is useful to a reader. The two can share a database, or use different stores, while still having different models. On this page Start from the question Commands communicate intent Read models communicate useful facts Handle the gap between writes and reads Avoid expensive read paths 
 In Troolio, an event-sourced actor is a natural command boundary. A query to that actor reads its current reconstructed state. A projection can also produce a SQL view that answers cross-actor questions without loading many actors. 
 Start from the question 
 A workshop application has several readers: 
 
 
 
 Question 
 Suitable model 
 
 
 
 
 What is the status of this one registration? 
 A registration actor query or an exact registration card read. 
 
 
 Show my registrations for this workshop 
 An indexed SQL view filtered by current user and workshop. 
 
 
 How many places can still be allocated safely? 
 The authoritative write-side capacity decision. 
 
 
 Show activity across all workshops 
 A separate reporting projection with paging and access control. 
 
 
 
 The same event can update more than one view. There is no need to expose a complete actor snapshot when the page only needs a name, status, and workshop ID. 
 Commands communicate intent 
 The sample makes registration and cancellation explicit commands. It records accepted outcomes as past-tense events. 
 public interface IRegistrationActor : IActor { }

[GenerateSerializer]
public record RequestRegistration(Metadata Headers, Guid RegistrationId,
    Guid WorkshopId, string DisplayName) : Command<IRegistrationActor>(Headers);

[GenerateSerializer]
public record CancelRegistration(Metadata Headers) : Command<IRegistrationActor>(Headers);

[GenerateSerializer]
public record GetRegistration : Query<IRegistrationActor, RegistrationState>;

[GenerateSerializer]
public record RegistrationRequested(Metadata Headers, Guid RegistrationId,
    Guid WorkshopId, Guid AttendeeId, string DisplayName) : Event(Headers);

[GenerateSerializer]
public record RegistrationCancelled(Metadata Headers, Guid RegistrationId,
    Guid WorkshopId, Guid AttendeeId, string DisplayName) : Event(Headers);
 
 A command can fail because its inputs or current state are invalid. A query should not create a registration as a side effect. Make the API outcome clear enough that the client knows whether a request was rejected, accepted for processing, or committed under the selected protocol. 
 Read models communicate useful facts 
 A registration card is a deliberately small result: 
 public sealed record RegistrationCard(Guid RegistrationId, Guid WorkshopId,
    Guid AttendeeId, string DisplayName, string Status);
 
 The SQL reader filters by the current authenticated user in the query itself. It does not load every card and filter the result in memory. For a list, choose an index and stable ordering that match the question, and return a bounded page with a continuation cursor. 
 Microsoft's CQRS guidance  describes the distinction between read and write models and the consistency consequences of separately updated stores. Use this pattern where the different responsibilities are useful; the actor and provider contracts determine your application's actual guarantees. 
 Handle the gap between writes and reads 
 A command may commit before the SQL card changes. Tell callers what that means. A UI can display the accepted command result, show a short updating state, then refresh the view when its projection is current. A stale view should not be silently used as authority for a conflicting command. 
 A returned source version can help a client track the update of one source stream. It is not a total ordering across unrelated actors. If a page depends on several streams, define a version vector, operation receipt, or other freshness contract appropriate to that page. 
 Avoid expensive read paths 
 A cross-actor catalogue should not reconstruct every actor on each API request. A growing history can turn a once-small replay query into a slow endpoint. Promote that view into an application-owned durable projection, index it, and run any catch-up as bounded work. 
 An exact read of one small linked-event model can still be useful.  Read-model design  explains the current Troolio resolver and why it is a different serving choice from a SQL catalogue. 
 Continue with  projection design ,  realtime updates , and  actor boundaries .

title: Replay and live events
description: Keep state restoration pure and give projection repair its own bounded pipeline.
text:
Replay and live events 
 An event appears in two different situations. An actor applies a newly decided event during command processing, and it applies historical events when restoring state. The state calculation should produce the same result in either situation. Work that reaches another system needs a separate live delivery and recovery path. On this page A pure state transition Live subscribers have a different responsibility Rebuilds are explicit work Snapshots have a narrower purpose Startup and readiness 
 If a handler sends a confirmation whenever it sees  RegistrationRequested , activating the actor can send confirmations for old registrations. A process restart becomes visible to customers. Keeping event handlers pure prevents that error. 
 
 A pure state transition 
 The sample represents its current registration state as an immutable record. Applying an event returns another record and does not perform I/O. 
 [GenerateSerializer]
public record RegistrationState(Guid RegistrationId, Guid WorkshopId,
    Guid AttendeeId, string DisplayName, string Status) : IActorState
{
    public static RegistrationState Empty => new(Guid.Empty, Guid.Empty,
        Guid.Empty, "", "absent");

    public RegistrationState Apply(RegistrationRequested e) =>
        new(e.RegistrationId, e.WorkshopId, e.AttendeeId, e.DisplayName, "requested");

    public RegistrationState Apply(RegistrationCancelled e) =>
        new(e.RegistrationId, e.WorkshopId, e.AttendeeId, e.DisplayName, "cancelled");
}
 
 The actor's  On  methods assign the returned value. They do not issue commands to the roster actor, write SQL, or call a notification provider. Historical replay can therefore restore a cancelled registration without repeating the cancellation's downstream work. 
 A command handler is different: it considers current state, validates intent, and decides events. It should not change state by mutating fields before producing the accepted event. The event application remains the common state transition path. 
 Live subscribers have a different responsibility 
 An orchestration listener reacts to an event by issuing another actor command. A projection listener writes a read model. Those consumers handle event delivery outside the owning actor's replay handler. Whether and when they run relative to a transaction depends on the route and provider. 
 For a durable projection route, committed events must retain recoverable handoff work. A worker can redeliver that source after failure, so the consumer should recognize source identity and apply its changes idempotently.  Projection design  follows that pipeline. 
 Do not manually publish every replayed event to all live subscribers merely to make SQL look current. It mixes restoration, data repair, and side effects, and can duplicate notifications or orchestrated actions. 
 Rebuilds are explicit work 
 Sometimes a new projection needs historical data. Run an explicit rebuild consumer with a versioned projection name, target schema, and durable progress. Read verified source data in bounded pages. Apply it through the same pure mapper, and preserve the isolation of unrelated partitions. 
 A rebuild of a display view should not execute the business orchestration listeners or send confirmations. Treat “reconstruct the read side” as its own task. Decide how live updates are caught up before promoting the rebuilt model. 
 Snapshots have a narrower purpose 
 A snapshot can reduce actor state replay work when the selected store and actor path support it. It does not populate your SQL read models, establish caller authorization, or certify that an unrelated consumer has processed events. Current authority-sensitive source-observation routes may bypass legacy snapshots. 
 Keep snapshot policy tied to the actor's state schema and committed history. Verify replay behavior with old events before changing a state record or serializer. 
 Startup and readiness 
 A serving host can check cluster membership and required provider connectivity without replaying every domain stream. A global warm-up that loads every registration makes startup grow with the application's entire history and lets one malformed stream delay everyone. 
 Initialize services at startup; restore an actor when it is needed. Run catch-up separately and expose the affected projection's readiness and lag at the appropriate scope.  Projection catch-up  shows bounded progress and failure handling. 
 Continue with  read-model design ,  idempotency and ordering , and  testing applications .

title: Realtime read-model updates
description: Notify clients after projection commit and refresh through an authorized query.
text:
Realtime read-model updates 
 A command result and the read model shown by a browser can become current at different times. A push channel helps the UI learn that its view may have changed, then refresh through the normal authorized query path. On this page Publish after the read model commits Carry a small reference Close the initial subscription race Coalesce bursts Explain freshness to the user 
 The notification is a hint about committed data. It should not become an alternative authorization boundary or a claim that the browser already has the latest state. 
 
 Publish after the read model commits 
 A view writer first commits its SQL change and source receipt. The application can then make a hint available to clients. Publishing before commit can cause the client to read the old view and miss the actual update. 
 If reliable hint delivery matters, persist notification work with the projection transaction and let a worker deliver it. An in-process callback after commit can be lost on a crash. A periodic read fallback can make a hint-only transport useful while preserving the durable view as the source for readers. 
 Troolio does not choose the browser transport for you. Server-Sent Events, SignalR, WebSockets, or polling can be application choices, each with connection and reconnection behavior. 
 Carry a small reference 
 The workshop helper receives a registration reference and reads its SQL view using the current authenticated user: 
 public sealed record RegistrationChangedHint(Guid RegistrationId);

public static class RegistrationRefresh
{
    public static Task<RegistrationCard?> AfterHintAsync(RegistrationChangedHint hint,
        Guid authenticatedUserId, SqlRegistrationCards reader, CancellationToken cancellationToken) =>
        reader.GetForUserAsync(hint.RegistrationId, authenticatedUserId, cancellationToken);
}
 
 The hint does not include the attendee's display name or grant access to the registration. A missing or unauthorized row still produces no card. A user's access can change while a connection remains open, so the reader and streaming endpoint must apply the current access policy. 
 Use a projection version or source position in the hint only when the application has a clear comparison rule. Do not treat positions from unrelated streams as one global ordering. 
 Close the initial subscription race 
 A browser can miss an update if it reads the view and subscribes afterward. A safer opening sequence is: authorize the target, establish the subscription, then read the authoritative current view and send the first state/barrier. Later hints trigger another read. 
 If subscription setup fails, report that state rather than claiming the client is now receiving live updates. For an unreliable hint transport, a bounded refresh interval or reconnect read can compensate for missed hints. 
 Coalesce bursts 
 Several events may update one page in a short interval. A hint queue can coalesce repeated references so the browser makes one current read rather than issuing a query for every historical intermediate state. That suits a current-view UI; an audit timeline needs a different model if every transition must be displayed. 
 Bound subscriptions per session and process, close expired sessions, cancel work on disconnect, and unsubscribe during shutdown. Those limits protect both the transport and the database reader. They are application hosting decisions, not defaults supplied by a projection attribute. 
 Explain freshness to the user 
 A useful UI can show an accepted command immediately, then an updating indicator until the relevant view is current. Distinguish a slow projection from a failed command. A client timeout should lead to outcome reconciliation, not blind creation of another registration. 
 Continue with  CQRS in practice ,  projection design , and  read-model design .

title: Selected command route
description: Admission and planning for atomic command execution.
text:
Selected command route 
 A selected command route is an opt-in path for commands whose event writes and related handoffs must close together. It binds one authenticated operation to one root actor, a current deployment route, a complete event plan, and a capable store. Ordinary actor commands remain available; installing an adapter does not select this path. On this page From ingress to completion Route selection checklist Example: Bind a command identity 
 
 From ingress to completion 
 
 Authenticate the caller and authorize the command, actor, and route at ingress. The host supplies the current principal; message metadata alone is not authority. 
 Create or verify a stable operation ID and canonical request identity.  TrustedAtomicCommandIngressAdapter  and  TrustedAtomicCommandIdentityAuthority  describe this boundary. 
 Acquire the selected route lease and verify the current deployment epoch and fingerprint. Admission can reject a stale silo or an unreviewed actor/handler registration. 
 Plan the root event and any supported causal subscriber events while handlers remain free of external effects. Freeze a closed participant set before storage. 
 Commit with the route fence and expected versions. Return the durable completion receipt only after every required write and projection handoff commits. 
 
 The memory-only path has additional contextual contracts ( MemoryOnlySelectedCommandContext  and  IMemoryOnlyContextualAtomicEventTransactionStore ). “Memory-only” describes precommit planning, not disposable persistence. A failed planner cannot be recovered by replaying a side effect. 
 Route selection checklist 
 Select the route only after reviewing the actor and subscriber inventory, event serialization, store capabilities, recovery policy, provider idempotency, and retention window. Pin the selected deployment and keep the route fence current across promotion or rollback.  Atomic commit ,  route authority , and  recovery  provide the individual contracts. 
 Example: Bind a command identity 
 After authenticating and authorizing the caller, issue a claim from canonical command bytes. Keep the server key in trusted host configuration and reuse the same  operationId  for retries. 
 public static TrustedAtomicCommandIdentityClaim IssueIdentity(
    byte[] serverKey, Guid operationId, byte[] canonicalCommand) =>
    TrustedAtomicCommandIdentityAuthority.Issue(serverKey, operationId,
        "user-42", "CounterActor/42", nameof(Increment), canonicalCommand);
